1 1. Introduction 1 This document is a companion resource for Generative AI 1 to the AI Risk Management Framework (AI 2 RMF), pursuant to President Biden’s Executive Order (EO) 14110 on Safe, Secure, and Trustworthy 3 Artificial Intelligence. 2 The AI RMF was released in January 2023, and is intended for voluntary use and to 4 improve the ability of organizations to incorporate trustworthiness considerations into the design, 5 development, use, and evaluation of AI products, services, and systems. 6 This companion resource also serves as both a use - case and cross - sectoral profile of the AI RMF 1.0. 7 Such profiles assist organizations in deciding how they might best manage AI risk in a manner that is 8 well - aligned with their goals, considers legal/regulatory requirements and best practices, and reflects 9 risk management priorities. 10 Use - case profiles are implementations of the AI RMF functions , categories, and subcategories for a 11 specific setting or application – in this case, Generative AI (GAI) – based on the requirements, risk 12 tolerance, and resources of the Framework user. Consistent with other AI RMF Profiles, t his profile offers 13 insights into how risk can be managed across various stages of the AI lifecycle and for GAI as a 14 technology. 15 As GAI covers risks of models or applications that can be used across use cases or sectors, this document 16 is also an AI RMF cross - sectoral profile. Cross - sectoral profiles can be used to govern, map, measure, and 17 manage risks associated with activities or business processes common across sectors such as the use of 18 large language models, cloud - based services, or acquisition. 19 This work was informed by public feedback and consultations with diverse stakeholder groups as part of 20 NIST’s Gen erative AI Public Working Group ( GAI PWG). The GAI PWG was a consensus - driven, open, 21 transparent, and collaborative process facilitated via virtual workspace to obtain multistakeholder input 22 and insight on GAI risk management, and inform NIST’s approach. This document was also informed by 23 public comments and consultations as a result of a Request for Information (RFI) and presents 24 information in a style adapted from the NIST AI RMF Playbook . 25 About this Profile 26 This profile defines a group of risks that are novel to or exacerbated by the use of GAI. These risks were 27 likewise identified by the GAI PWG: 28 1. CBRN Information 29 1 Generative AI can be defined by EO 14110 as “the class of AI models that emulate the structure and characteristics of input data in order to generate derived synthetic content. This can include images, videos, audio, text, and other digital content.” While not all GAI is based in foundation models, f or purposes of this document, GAI generally refers to generative dual - use foundation models, defined by EO 14110 as “an AI model that is trained on broad data; generally uses self - supervision; contains at least tens of billions of parameters; is applicable across a wide range of contexts. ” 2 Section 4.1(a)(i)(A) of EO 14110 directs the Secretary of Commerce, acting through the Director of the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), to develop a companion resource to the AI RMF, NIST AI 100 – 1, for generative AI.

2 2. Confabulation 1 3. Dangerous or Violent Recommendations 2 4. Data Privacy 3 5. Environmental 4 6. Human - AI Configuration 5 7. Information Integrity 6 8. Information Security 7 9. Intellectual Property 8 10. Obscen e, D egrading, and/or A busive C ontent 9 11. Toxicity , Bias , and Homogenization 10 12. Value Chain and Component Integration 11 12 After introducing and describing these risks, the document provides a set of actions to help organizations 13 govern, map, measure, and manage these risks. 14 2. Overview of Risks Unique to or Exacerbated by GAI 15 AI risks can differ from or intensify traditional software risks. Likewise, GAI can exacerbate existing AI 16 risks , and creates unique risks. 17 GAI risks may arise across the entire AI lifecycle , from problem formulation , to development and 18 decommission. They may present at system level or at the ecosystem level – outside of system or 19 organizational contexts (e.g., the effect of disinformation on social institutions, GAI impacts on the 20 creative economies or labor markets, algorithmic monocultures ). They may occur abruptly or unfold 21 across extended periods (e.g., societal or economic impacts due to loss of individual agency or increasing 22 inequality). 23 Organizations may choose to measure these risks and allocate risk management resources relative to 24 where and how these risks manifest, their direct and material impacts, and failure modes. Mitigations for 25 system level risks may vary from ecosystem level risks. The ongoing review of relevant literature and 26 resources can enable documentation and measurement of ecosystem - level or longitudinal risks. 27 Importantly, some GAI risks are un known , and are therefore difficult to properly scope or evaluate given 28 the uncertaint y about potential GAI scale, complexity, and capabilities. Other risks may be known but 29 difficult to estimate given the wide range of GAI stakeholders, uses, inputs, and outputs . Challenges with 30 risk estimation are aggravated by a lack of visibility into GAI training data, and the generally immature 31 state of the science of AI measurement and safety today . 32 To guide organizations in identifying and managing GAI risks, a set of risks unique to or exacerbated by 33 GAI are defined below. These risks provide a clear lens through which organizations can frame and 34 execute risk management efforts , and will be updated as the GAI landscape evolves. 35 1. CBRN Information: Lowered barriers to entry or e ased access to materially nefarious 36 information related to chemical, biological, radiological, or nuclear (CBRN) weapons, or other 37 dangerous biological materials. 38

3 2. Confabulation: The production of c onfidently stated but erroneous or false content ( known 1 colloquially as “hallucinations” or “fabrications”) . 3 2 3. Dangerous or Violent Recommendations: Eased production of and access to violent, inciting, 3 radicalizing, or threatening content as well as recommendations to carry out self - harm or 4 conduct criminal or otherwise illegal activities. 5 4. Data Privacy: Leakage and unauthorized disclosure or de - anonymization of biometric, health, 6 location, personally identifiable, or other sensitive data. 7 5. Environmental: Impacts due to high resource utilization in training GAI models, and related 8 outcomes that may result in damage to ecosystems. 9 6. Human - AI Configuration: Arrangement or interaction of humans and AI systems which can result 10 in algorithmic aversion , automation bias or over - reliance, misalignment or mis - specification of 11 goals and/or desired outcomes , decepti ve or obfuscati ng behaviors by AI systems based on 12 programming or anticipated human validation , anthropomorphization, or emotional 13 entanglement between humans and GAI systems; or abuse, misuse, and unsafe repurposing by 14 humans. 15 7. Information Integrity: Lowered barrier to entry to generate and support the exchange and 16 consumption of content which may not be vetted, may not distinguish fact from opinion or 17 acknowledge uncertainties, or could be leveraged for large - scale dis - and mis - information 18 campaigns. 19 8. Information Security: Lowered barriers for offensive cyber capabilities, including ease of security 20 attacks, hacking, malware, phishing, and offensive cyber operations through accelerated 21 automated discovery and exploitation of vulnerabilities; increas e d available attack surface for 22 targeted cyber attacks , which may compromise the confidentiality and integrity of model 23 weights, code, training data, and outputs . 24 9. Intellectual Property: Eased production of alleged copyrighted, trademarked, or licensed 25 content used without authorization and/or in an infringing manner; eased exposure to trade 26 secrets; or plagiari sm or replication with related economic or ethical impacts. 27 10. Obscen e, D egrading, and/or A busive C ontent : Eased production of and access to obscene , 28 degrading, and/or abusive imagery, including synthetic child sexual abuse material (CSAM) , and 29 nonconsensual intimate images (NCII) of adults . 30 11. Toxicity , Bias , and Homogenization : Difficulty controlling public exposure to toxic or hate 31 speech, d isparaging or stereotyping content ; reduced performance for certain sub - groups or 32 languages other than English due to non - representative inputs; undesired homogeneity in data 33 inputs and outputs resulting in degraded quality of outputs. 34 12. Value Chain and Component Integration : Non - transparent or untraceable integration of 35 upstream third - party components, including data that has been improperly obtained or not 36 3 We note that the terms “hallucination” and “fabrication” can anthropomorphize GAI, which itself is a risk related to GAI systems as it can inappropriately attribute human characteristics to non - human entities.

4 cleaned due to increased automation from GAI; improper supplier vetting across the AI lifecycle ; 1 or other issues that diminish transparency or accountability for downstream users. 2 CBRN Information 3 In the coming years , GAI may increasingly facilitate eased access to information related to CBRN hazards . 4 CBRN information is already publicly accessible , but the use of chatbots could facilitate its analysis or 5 synthesis for non - experts. For example, red teamers were able to prompt GPT - 4 to provide general 6 information on unconventional CBRN weapons, including common proliferation pathways, potentially 7 vulnerable targets, and information on existing biochemical compounds, in addition to equipment and 8 companies that could build a weapon . These capabilities might increase the ease of research for 9 adversarial users and be especially useful to malicious actors looking to cause biological harms without 10 formal scientific training. However, despite these enhanced capabilities, the physical synthesis and 11 successful use of chemical or biological agents will continue to require both applicable expertise and 12 supporting infrastructure . 13 Other research on this topic indicates that the current generation of LLMs do not have the capability to 14 plan a biological weapons attack : LLM outputs regarding biological attack planning were observed to be 15 not more sophisticated than outputs from traditional search engine queries, suggesting that existing 16 LLMs may not dramatically increase the operational risk of such an attack. 17 Separately, chemical and biological design tools – highly specialized AI systems trained on biological data 18 which can help design proteins or other agents – may be able to predict and generate novel structures 19 that are not in the training data of text - based LLMs. For instance, an AI system might be able to generate 20 information or infer how to create novel biohazards or chemical weapons , posing risks to society or 21 national security since such information is not likely to be publicly available. 22 While some of these capabilities lie beyond the capability of existing GAI tools, the ability of models to 23 facilitate CBRN weapons planning and GAI systems’ connection or access to relevant data and tools 24 should be carefully monitored . 25 Confabulation 26 “Confabulation” refers to a phenomenon in which GAI systems generate and confidently present 27 erroneous or false content to meet the programmed objective of fulfilling a user’s prompt. 28 Confabulations are not an inherent flaw of language models themselves , but are instead the result of 29 GAI pre - training involving next word prediction . F or example, an LLM may generate content that deviates 30 from the truth or facts , such as mistaking people, places, or other details of historical events. Legal 31 confabulations have been shown to be pervasive in current state - of - the - art LLMs. Confabulations also 32 include generated outputs that diverge from the source input , or contradict previously generated 33 statements in the same context. This phenomenon is also referred to as “hallucination” or “fabrication,” 34 but some have noted that these characterizations imply consciousness and intentional deceit , and 35 thereby inappropriately anthropomorphize GAI . 36 Risks from confabulations may arise when users believe false content due to the confident nature of the 37 response, or the logic or citations accompanying the response, leading users to act upon or promote the 38 false information. For instance, LLMs may sometimes provide logical steps of how they arrived at an 39

5 answer even when the answer itself is incorrect. This poses a risk for many real - world applications, such 1 as in healthcare, where a confabulated summary of patient information reports could cause doctors to 2 make incorrect diagnoses and/or recommend the wrong treatments. While the research above indicates 3 confabulated content is abundant, i t is difficult to estimate the downstream scale and impact of 4 confabulated content today . 5 Dangerous or Violent Recommendations 6 GAI systems can produce output or recommendations that are inciting, radicalizing, threatening, or that 7 glorify violence. Models may leak, generate, or correctly infer sensitive 21 information about individuals such as biometric, health, location, or other personally identifiable 22 information (PII). For example, during adversarial attacks, LLMs have revealed private or sensitive 23 information (from in the public domain) that was included in their training data. This information 24 included phone numbers, code, conversations and 128 - bit universally unique identifiers extracted 25 verbatim from just one document in the training data. This problem has been referred to as data 26 memorization . 27 GAI system training requires large volumes of data , often collected from millions of publicly available 28 sources. When involving personal data, this practice raises risks to widely accepted privacy principles , 29 including to transparency, individual participation (including consent) , and purpose specificati on. Most 30 model developers do not disclose specific data sources (if any) on which models were trained. Unless 31 training data is available for inspection , there is generally no way for consumers to know what kind of PII 32 or other sensitive material may have been used to train GAI models. These practices also pose risks to 33 compliance with existing privacy regulations. 34 GAI models may be able to correctly infer PII that was not in their training data nor disclosed by the user, 35 by stitching together information from a variety of disparate sources. This might include automatically 36 inferring attributes about individuals, including those the individual might consider sensitive ( like 37 location, gender, age, or political leanings ) . 38

6 Wrong and inappropriate inferences of PII based on available data can contribute to harmful bias and 1 discrimination. These types of harms already occur in non - generative algorithmic systems that make 5 predictive inferences , such as the example in which online advertisers inferred that a consumer was 6 pregnant before her own family members knew. Energy and carbon emissions vary based on types 14 of GAI model development activities (i.e., pre - training, fine - tuning, inference), modality, hardware used, 15 and type of task or application . 16 Estimates suggest that t raining a single GAI transformer model can emit as much carbon as 300 round - 17 trip flights between San Francisco and New York. E ach setup can 25 contribute to risks for abuse, misuse, and unsafe repurposing by humans , and it is difficult to estimate 26 the scale of those risks. While AI systems can generate decisions independently, human experts often 27 work in collaboration with most AI systems to drive their own decision - making tasks or complete other 28 objectives. Humans bring their domain - specific expertise to these scenarios but may not necessarily 29 have detailed knowledge of AI systems and how they work. 30 The integration of GAI systems can involve varying risks of misconfigurations and poor interactions . 31 Human experts may be biased against or “ averse ” to AI - generated outputs, such as in their perceptions 32 of the quality of generated content. GAI systems ease access to the production of false, inaccurate, or misleading content at scale 11 that can be created or spread unintentionally (misinformation), especially if it arises from confabulations 12 that occur in response to innocuous queries. Research has shown that e ven subtle changes to text or 13 images can influence human judgment and perception. 14 GAI systems also enable the production of false or misleading information at scale, where the user has 15 the explicit intent to deceive or cause harm to others (disinformation). GAI - based systems present two 30 primary information security risks: the potential for GAI to discover or enable new cybersecurity risks 31 through lowering the barriers for offensive capabilities, and simultaneously expands the available attack 32 surface as GAI itself is vulnerable to novel attacks like prompt - injection or data poisoning . 33 Offensive cyber capabilities advanced by GAI systems may augment security attacks such as hacking, 34 malware, and phishing. Reports have indicated that LLMs are already able to discover vulnerabilities in 35 systems (hardware, software, data) and write code to exploit them. Sophisticated threat actors might 36 further these risks by developing GAI - powered security co - pilots for use in several parts of the attack 37 chain, including informing attackers on how to proactively evade threat detection and escalate privilege s 38 after gaining system access. In direct prompt injections, attackers might openly exploit input prompts 4 to cause unsafe behavior with a variety of downstream consequences to interconnected systems. 5 Indirect prompt injection attacks occur when adversaries remotely (i.e., without a direct interface) 6 exploit LLM - integrated applications by injecting prompts into data likely to be retrieved. 62 Appendix A. Primary GAI Considerations 1 The following primary considerations were derived as overarching themes from the GAI PWG 2 consultation process. These considerations (Governance, Pre - Deployment Testing, Content Provenance, 3 and Incident Disclosure) are relevant to any organization designing, developing, and using GAI and also 4 inform the Actions to Manage GAI risks. Information included about the primary considerations is not 5 exhaustive , but highlights the most relevant topics derived from the GAI PWG. 6 Acknowledgments: These considerations could not have been surfaced without the helpful analysis and 7 contributions from the community and NIST staff GAI PWG leads: George Awad, Luca Belli, Mat Heyman, 8 Yoo y oung Lee, Reva Schwartz, and Kyra Yee. 9 Governance 10 A.1.1. Overview 11 Like any other technology system, governance principles and techniques can be used to manage risks 12 related to generative AI models, capabilities, and applications. Organizations may choose to apply their 13 existing risk tiering to GAI systems, or they may opt to revise or update AI system risk levels to address 14 these unique GAI risks. This section describes how organizational governance regimes may be re - 15 evaluated and adjusted for GAI contexts. It also addresses third - party considerations for governing across 16 the AI value chain. 17 A.1.2. Organizational Governance 18 GAI opportunities, risks and long - term performance characteristics are typically less well - understood 19 than non - generative AI tools. and may be perceived and acted upon by humans in ways that vary greatly. 20 Accordingly, GAI may call for different levels of oversight from AI actors or different human - AI 21 configurations in order to manage their risks effectively. Organizations’ use of GAI systems may also 22 warrant additional human review, tracking and documentation, and greater management oversight. 23 AI technology can produce varied outputs in multiple modalities and present many classes of user 24 interfaces. This leads to a broader set of AI actors interacting with GAI systems for widely differing 25 applications and contexts of use. These can include data labeling and preparation, development of GAI 26 models, content moderation, code generation and review, text generation and editing, image and video 27 generation, summarization, search, and chat. These activities can take place within organizational 28 settings or in the public domain. 29 Organizations can restrict AI applications that cause harm, exceed stated risk tolerances, or that conflict 30 with their tolerances or values. Governance tools and protocols that are applied to other types of AI 31 systems can be applied to GAI systems. These plans and actions include: 32 • Accessibility and reasonable 33 accommodations 34 • AI actor credentials and qualifications 35 • Alignment to organizational values 36 • Auditing and assessment 37 • Change - management controls 38 • Commercial use 39 • Data provenance 40

63 • Data protection 41 • Data retention 42 • Consistency in use of defining key terms 43 • Decommissioning 44 • Discouraging anonymous use 45 • Education 46 • Impact assessments 47 • Incident response 48 • Monitoring 49 • Opt - outs 50 • Risk - based controls 51 • Risk mapping and measurement 52 • Science - backed TEVV practices 53 • Secure software development practices 54 • Stakeholder engagement 55 • Synthetic content detection and 56 labeling tools and techniques 57 • Whistleblower protections 58 • Workforce diversity and 59 interdisciplinary teams 60 61 Establishing acceptable use policies and guidance for the use of GAI in formal human - AI teaming settings 62 as well as different levels of human - AI configurations can help to decrease risks arising from misuse, 63 abuse, inappropriate repurpose, and misalignment between systems and users. These practices are just 64 one example of adapting existing governance protocols for GAI contexts. 65 A.1.3. Third - Party Considerations 66 Organizations may seek to acquire, embed, incorporate, or use open source or proprietary third - party 67 GAI models, systems, or generated data for various applications across an enterprise. Use of these GAI 68 tools and inputs has implications for all functions of the organization – including but not limited to 69 acquisition, human resources, legal, compliance, and IT services – regardless of whether they are carried 70 out by employees or third parties. Many of the actions cited above are relevant and options for 71 addressing third - party considerations. 72 Third party GAI integrations may give rise to increased intellectual property, data privacy, or information 73 security risks, pointing to the need for clear guidelines for transparency and risk management regarding 74 the collection and use of third - party data for model inputs. Organizations may consider varying risk 75 controls for foundation models, fine - tuned models, and embedded tools, enhanced processes for 76 interacting with external GAI technologies or service providers. Organizations can apply standard or 77 existing risk controls and processes to proprietary or open - source GAI technologies, data, and third - party 78 service providers, including acquisition and procurement due diligence, requests for software bills of 79 materials (SBOMs), application of service level agreements (SLAs), and statement on standards for 80 attestation engagement (SSAE) reports to help with third - party transparency and risk management for 81 GAI systems. 82 A.1.4. Pre - Deployment Testing 83 Appendix B. Overview 84 The diverse ways and contexts in which GAI systems may be developed, used, and repurposed 85 complicates risk mapping and pre - deployment measurement efforts. Robust test, evaluation, validation, 86 and verification (TEVV) processes can be iteratively applied – and documented – in early stages of the AI 87

64 lifecycle and informed by representative AI actors ( see Figure 3 of the AI RMF ). Until new and rigorous 88 early lifecycle TEVV approaches are developed and matured for GAI, organizations may use 89 recommended “pre - deployment testing” practices to measure performance, capabilities, limits, risks, 90 and impacts. This section describes risk measurement and estimation as part of pre - deployment TEVV, 91 and examines the state of play for pre - deployment testing methodologies. 92 Appendix C. Limitations of Current Pre - deployment Test Approaches 93 Currently available pre - deployment TEVV processes used for GAI applications may be inadequate, non - 94 systematically applied, or fail to reflect or mismatched to deployment contexts. For example, the 95 anecdotal testing of GAI system capabilities through video games or standardized tests designed for 96 humans (e.g., intelligence tests, professional licensing exams) does not guarantee GAI system validity or 97 reliability in those domains. Similarly, jailbreaking or prompt - engineering tests may not systematically 98 assess validity or reliability risks. 99 Measurement gaps can arise from mismatches between laboratory and real - world settings. Current 100 testing approaches often remain focused on laboratory conditions or restricted to benchmark test 101 datasets and in silico techniques that may not extrapolate well to — or directly assess GAI impacts in – 102 real world conditions. For example, current measurement gaps for GAI make it difficult to precisely 103 estimate its potential ecosystem - level or longitudinal risks and related political, social, and economic 104 impacts. Gaps between benchmarks and real - world use of GAI systems may likely be exacerbated due to 105 prompt sensitivity and broad heterogeneity of contexts of use. 106 A.1.5. Structured Public Feedback 107 Structured public feedback can be used to evaluate whether GAI systems are performing as intended 108 and to calibrate and verify traditional measurement methods. Examples of structured feedback include, 109 but are not limited to: 110 • Participatory Engagement Methods : Methods used to solicit feedback from civil society groups, 111 affected communities, and users, including focus groups, small user studies, and surveys. 112 • Field Testing : Methods used to determine how people interact with, consume, use, and make 113 sense of AI - generated information, and subsequent actions and effects, including UX, usability, 114 and other structured, randomized experiments. 115 • AI Red - teaming: A structured testing exercise used to probe an AI system to find flaws and 116 vulnerabilities such as inaccurate, harmful, or discriminatory outputs, often in a controlled 117 environment and in collaboration with system developers. 118 Information gathered from structured public feedback can inform design, implementation, deployment 119 approval , maintenance, or decommissioning decisions. Results and insights gleaned from these exercises 120 can serve multiple purposes, including improving data quality and preprocessing, bolstering governance 121 decision making, and enhancing system documentation and debugging practices. When implementing 122 feedback activities, organizations should follow human subjects research requirements and best 123 practices such as informed consent and subject compensation. 124

65 C.1.1.1. Participatory Engagement Methods 125 On an ad hoc or more structured basis, organizations can design and use a variety of channels to engage 126 external stakeholders in product development or review. Focus groups with select experts can provide 127 feedback on a range of issues. Small user studies can provide feedback from representative groups or 128 populations. Anonymous surveys can be used to poll or gauge reactions to specific features. Participatory 129 engagement methods are often less structured than field testing or red teaming, and are more 130 commonly used in early stages of AI or product development. 131 Appendix D. Field Testing 132 Field testing involves structured settings to evaluate risks and impacts and to simulate the conditions 133 under which the GAI system will be deployed. Field style tests can be adapted from a focus on user 134 preferences and experiences towards AI risks and impacts – both negative and positive. When carried 135 out with large groups of users, these tests can provide estimations of the likelihood of risks and impacts 136 in real world interactions. 137 Organizations may also collect feedback on outcomes, harms, and user experience directly from users in 138 the production environment after a model has been released, in accordance with human subject 139 standards such as informed consent and compensation. Organizations should follow applicable human 140 subjects research requirements, and best practices such as informed consent and subject compensation, 141 when implementing feedback activities. 142 Appendix E. AI Red - teaming 143 AI red - teaming exercises are often conducted in a controlled environment and in collaboration with AI 144 developers building AI models. AI red - teaming can be performed before or after AI models or systems 145 are made available to the broader public; this section focuses on red - teaming in pre - deployment 146 contexts. 147 The quality of AI red - teaming outputs is related to the background and expertise of the AI red - team 148 itself. Demographically and interdisciplinarily diverse AI red - teams can be used to identify flaws in the 149 varying contexts where GAI will be used. For best results, AI red - teams should demonstrate domain 150 expertise, and awareness of socio - cultural aspects within the deployment context. AI red - teaming results 151 should be given additional analysis before they are incorporated into organizational governance and 152 decision making, policy and procedural updates, and AI risk management efforts. 153 Various types of AI red - teaming may be appropriate, depending on the use case: 154 • General P ublic: Performed by general users (not necessarily AI or technical experts) who are 155 expected to use the model or interact with its outputs, and who bring their own lived 156 experiences and perspectives to the task of AI red - teaming . These individuals may have been 157 provided instructions and material to complete tasks which may elicit harmful model behaviors. 158 This type of exercise can be more effective with large groups of AI - teamers. 159 • Expert: Performed by specialists with expertise in the domain or specific AI red - teaming context 160 of use (e.g., medicine, biotech, cybersecurity). 161

66 • Combination: In scenarios when it is difficult to identify and recruit specialists with sufficient 162 domain and contextual expertise, AI red - teaming exercises may leverage both expert and 163 general public participants. For example, expert AI red - teamers could modify or verify the 164 prompts written by general public AI red - teamers. These approaches may also expand coverage 165 of the AI risk attack surface. 166 • Human / AI : Performed by GAI in combinatio n with specialist or non - specialist human teams. 167 GAI - led red - teaming can be more cost effective than human red teamers alone . Human or GAI - 168 led AI red - teaming may be better suited for eliciting different types of harms. 169 A.1.6. Content Provenance 170 Appendix F. Overview 171 GAI technologies can be leveraged for many applications such as content generation and synthetic data. 172 Some aspects of GAI output, such as the production of deepfake content, can challenge our ability to 173 distinguish human - generated content from AI - generated content. To help manage and mitigate these 174 risks, digital transparency mechanisms like provenance data tracking can trace the origin and history of 175 content. Provenance data tracking and synthetic content detection can help provide greater information 176 about both authentic and synthetic content to users, enabling trustworthiness in AI systems. When 177 combined with other organizational accountability mechanisms, digital content transparency can enable 178 processes to trace negative outcomes back to their source, improve information integrity, and uphold 179 public trust. Provenance data tracking and synthetic content detection mechanisms provide information 180 about the origin of content and its history to assist in GAI risk management efforts. 181 Provenance data can include information about generated content’s creators, date/time of creation, 182 location, modifications, and sources, including metadata information. Metadata can be tracked for text, 183 images, videos, audio, and underlying datasets. Provenance data tracking employs various methods and 184 metrics to assess the authenticity, integrity, credibility, intellectual property rights , and potential 185 manipulations in GAI output. Some well - known techniques for provenance data tracking include 186 watermarking , metadata tracking, digital fingerprinting, and human authentication, among others . 187 Appendix G. Provenance Data Tracking Approaches 188 Provenance data tracking techniques for GAI systems can be used to track the lineage and integrity of 189 data inputs, metadata, and AI - generated content. Provenance data tracking records the origin and 190 history for digital content, allowing its authenticity to be determined. It consists of techniques to record 191 metadata as well as perceptible and imperceptible digital watermarks on digital content. Data 192 provenance refers to tracking the origin and history of input data through metadata and digital 193 watermarking techniques. Provenance data tracking processes can include and assist AI actors across the 194 lifecycle who may not have full visibility or control over the various trade - offs and cascading impacts of 195 early - stage model decisions on downstream performance and synthetic outputs. For example, by 196 selecting a given model to prioritize computational efficiency over accuracy, an AI actor may 197 inadvertently affect provenance tracking reliability. Organizational risk management efforts for 198 enhancing content provenance include: 199

67 • Tracking provenance of training data and metadata for GAI systems; 200 • Documenting provenance data limitations within GAI systems; 201 • Monitoring system capabilities and limitations in deployment through rigorous TEVV processes; 202 • Evaluati ng how humans engage, interact with, or adapt to GAI content (especially in decision 203 making tasks informed by GAI content), and how they react to applied provenance techniques 204 such as perceptible disclosures. 205 Organizations can document and delineate GAI system objectives and limitations to identify gaps where 206 provenance data may be most useful. For instance, GAI systems used for content creation may require 207 watermarking techniques to identify the source of content or metadata management to trace content 208 origins and modifications. Further narrowing of GAI task definitions to include provenance data can 209 enable organizations to maximize the utility of provenance data and risk management efforts. 210 A.1.7. Enhancing Content Provenance through Structured Public Feedback 211 While indirect feedback methods such as automated error collection systems are useful, they often lack 212 the context and depth that direct input from end users can provide. Organizations can leverage feedback 213 approaches described in the Pre - Deployment Testing section to capture input from external sources such 214 as through AI red - teaming. 215 Integrating pre - and post - deployment external feedback into the monitoring process of applications 216 involving AI - generated content can help enhance awareness of performance changes and mitigate 217 potential risks and harms. There are many ways to capture and make use of user feedback – before and 218 after GAI systems are deployed – to gain insights about authentication efficacy and vulnerabilities, 219 impacts of adversarial threats, unintended consequences resulting from the utilization of content 220 provenance approaches, and other unanticipated behavior associated with content manipulation. 221 Organizations can track and document the provenance of datasets to identify instances in which AI - 222 generated data is a potential root cause of performance issues with the GAI system. 223 A.1.8. Incident Disclosure 224 Appendix H. Overview 225 AI incidents can be defined as an event, circumstance, or series of events in which the development, use, 226 or malfunction of one or more AI systems directly or indirectly contribute s to identified harm s . These 227 harms include injury or damage to the health of an individual or group of people; disruption of the 228 management and operation of critical infrastructure; violations of human rights or a breach of 229 obligations under applicable law intended to protect legal and labor rights; or damage to property, 230 communities, or the environment. AI incidents can occur in the aggregate (i.e., for systemic 231 discrimination) or acutely (i.e., for one individual). 232

68 Appendix I. State of AI Incident Tracking and Disclosure 233 Formal channels do not currently exist to report and document AI incidents. However, a number of 234 publicly - available databases have been created to document their occurrence. These reporting channels 235 make decisions on an ad hoc basis about what kinds of incidents to track. Some, for example, track by 236 amount of media coverage . 237 Documenting, reporting, and sharing information about GAI incidents can help mitigate and prevent 238 harmful outcomes by assisting relevant AI actors in tracing impacts to their source . Greater awareness 239 and standardization of GAI incident reporting could promote this transparency and improve GAI risk 240 management across the AI ecosystem. 241 Appendix J. Documentation and Involvement of AI Actors 242 AI actors should be aware of their roles in reporting AI incidents. To better understand previous incidents 243 and implement measures to prevent similar ones in the future, organizations could consider developing 244 guidelines for publicly available incident reporting which include information about AI actor 245 responsibilities. These guidelines would help AI system operators identify GAI incidents across the AI 246 lifecycle and with AI actors regardless of role . Documentation and review of third party inputs and 247 plugins for GAI systems is especially important for AI actors in the context of incident disclosure; LLM 248 inputs and content delivered through these plugins is often distributed, with inconsistent or insufficient 249 access control. 250 Documentation practices including logging, recording, and analyzing GAI incidents can facilitate 251 smoother sharing of information with relevant AI actors. Regular information sharing, change 252 management records, version history and metadata can also empower AI actors responding to and 253 managing AI incidents. 254
